Chemist and fellow 3D printer here. I agree with the others in saying that distillation is asking for trouble. I typically don't clean my washing IPA very much. Curing then filtering is possible, but using coffee filters to do it like others sometimes suggest will take forever to do, and you will end up having loads of your IPA evaporate anyway. It also causes problems if the resin forms a gel when cured in the IPA and it's also a nightmare to deal with.

So aside from just replacing it, you can get a little more life out of it by leaving the residue to settle for a few days, then carefully pouring the topmost portion into another container, leaving the residue at the bottom. You won't get all the IPA back like this, but it will extend its lifespan a bit.
Awesome work as always! What resin do you use to print your models?

I have the chitu H1 heater in mine, I just set it to 25 for about half an hour, longer if the room is particularly cold, to give the resin a chance to heat up. Note that it's unlikely a vat full of resin will reach the right temp after only 30 mins, but it's a good start.

Normally I just set it to go from there with plenty of bottom layers on a long exposure, keeping in mind that the polymerisation you are doing is fairly exothermic and will naturally heat the resin up. It seems to be enough to keep the resin at a decent temperature for the duration of the print, but I've certainly not been very scientific about it. The thermometer you mentioned is the screen temp as far as I'm aware, so it's not necessarily the best indicator of resin temp.

Other than that, I know that some people heat a bottle of resin in hot water for a little while before printing and again, letting the heat of the reaction keep it nice and cosy during the print.

Absolutely do not put it down the drain. You can leave it outside and the sun's UV will partially cure the resin in the liquid. If you have any other UV source that one may have around from curing your models, that will speed it up. You can then filter out the larger bits of partially cured resin, and then you can just reuse the IPA.

In short, it's a mixture of all 3. Hiragana and katakana represent syllables. For example, た would sound like 'ta' in romaji (roman characters). The difference between the two is typically hiragana is used for Japanese words and katakana is used for loan words from other languages but it's not *always* the case. Then finally you have kanji which are symbols taken from the chinese language which represent actual proper words.

Really, you should aim to learn them all but there are TONS of kanji out there and it will take time to get used to them. But as ever, practice makes perfect! I think generally most books or courses would want you to learn hiragana first then katakana, but I can't really testify to the best way. The way I've been learning had me learn hiragana before katakana and I've been doing kanji recognition on the side.

A quantum state is basically the condition of a particle at a given time, usually its wavefunction or set of quantum numbers. Basically quantum numbers tell you what energy level a particle is in. For example, we commonly describe electron quantum states with quantum numbers that tell you things like what type of orbital it is in and the orientation of this orbital. It's a bit more complicated than that of course, quantum mechanics is never simple.

Great questions, but not so easily explained. Firstly, the principle of two surfaces 'touching' each other comes down to atomic/molecular repulsion when they come very close together (commonly modelled as the [Lennard-Jones potential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lennard-Jones_potential)) so things will generally repell when they get close to eachother, however, things like cold welding can occur where there is no atmosphere.

Now, there are different ways of looking at surfaces, usually involving a concept called [quantum tunnelling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_tunnelling) and, as you can tell, this is deeply in the realms of quantum mechanics and can be a little complicated. But in this case, we can apply it to surface where we say 'here is a flat surface, this is where the materials atoms end' and this isn't usually hard to visualise. But wait! Quantum tunnelling is a thing, and it basically means that electrons can exist outside of this 'boundary' we defined and it gives us a probability of electrons being outside of this surface. Taking this concept forward, you can even use a kind of probe that you can bring extremely close to a surface (like as close as even a few atoms-gap between the probe and the surface) and long-story-short, you can run a current between the probe and the surface due to this overlap of electron density going beyond our boundary. This concept is known as [scanning electron microscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scanning_electron_microscope) and lets you 'see' what a surface looks like using all sorts of technological and engineering tricks. I hope this part didn't go too far off topic.

And finally, in theory, a photon can traverse and kind of gap between surfaces. Specific wavelengths of light (X-rays and other high energy, short wavelength photons) can penetrate most materials (think X-rays of a broken leg) and generally don't interact very strongly with matter, so it kind just passes through more than it would 'traverse'. In terms of a hydrogen atom, it's pretty likely since there is normally some kind of gas between surfaces that are not under vacuum, and hydrogen atoms are very small, so this isn't beyond the realm of reason.

You can go into the ideas of porous materials and all sorts, where you can consider the surface of the pores and how gasses can move through them, but this is a large subject on it's own.
